newsitem.title: UK: Bruton calls for review of Bloody Sunday tragedy.
newsitem.headline: Bruton calls for review of Bloody Sunday tragedy.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton called on Tuesday for a review of the 1972 'Bloody Sunday' killings of protesters in Northern Ireland after a British paratrooper said shameful and disgraceful acts had occurred.
In an interview from Washington, Bruton said new evidence about the killing of 13 unarmed demonstrators 25 years ago should be investigated.

"These statements are so specific that they must either be comprehensively and credibly rebutted which I believe is unlikely to be possible, or alternatively they must be thoroughly investigated," he told Channel 4 television news.
Bruton also said that a soldier's claim that a statement prepared for a 1972 investigation by Chief Justice Lord Widgery had been essentially changed by a superior was also extremely worrying.

Bruton's remarks followed a television interview with an unidentified British paratooper who recounted the events that led to the killings in Londonderrry during a demonstration in support of civil rights grievances by Northern Ireland's Catholic minority.

"It was certailnly the case that soldiers who had became involved in the shooting were in a situation where command and control was absent for a period of perhaps 15 minutes during which the shooting occurred," he told Channel 4 news.
"During that period of gunfire a number of fairly unfortunate, to say the least, decisions were made on the ground which led to some shameful and disgraceful acts being perpetrated."
Bruton, who was in Washington for St Patrick's Day celebrations, said the new information would form an important part of a dossier that his government would present to Britain.

Ireland was also studying evidence from a British soldier who told Ireland's Sunday Business Post that troops sent to Londondery to quell demonstrations by Catholic Irish nationalists were told to shoot to kill and ignored orders to stop shooting.
The man, identified as Soldier A, quoted an officer as telling his platoon: "Let's teach these buggers a lesson - we want some kills tomorrow."
He also said that even after an order to cease fire was given, some soldiers continued to fire on the civilians.

The official Widgery Tribunal that investigated the killings exonerated the paratroopers and accepted their version that they believed they were under fire from Irish Republican Army (IRA) gunmen fighting British rule.

Soldier A said the evidence he planned to give to the Widgery Tribunal was torn up by a British official and he was given another statement "which bore no relation to the facts" to give to the investigation.
Britain has refused to reopen a new inquiry into the tragedy unless new evidence is presented.

"I have no reason to believe but that the British government will look at it (the new evidence) objectively and if a full, sworn inquiry is the appropriate action, that action will be taken," Bruton said
